label: Laws of War and International Criminal Law

lessons.title: Jus ad Bellum and Jus in Bello: Two Separate Questions
body: The law of armed conflict is built on a deliberate separation. Jus ad bellum (the law on the resort to force) asks whether a state may use armed force against another state in the first place. Jus in bello (the law in war, today usually called international humanitarian law or IHL) asks how force may be used once hostilities exist, and how the people caught up in them must be treated. A third, newer label, jus post bellum, is sometimes used for the law of transition after conflict, though it is less settled as a distinct field.

Jus ad bellum is now centred on the UN Charter. Article 2(4) obliges members to refrain from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. There are two main exceptions. Article 51 preserves the inherent right of individual or collective self-defence if an armed attack occurs, and Chapter VII lets the Security Council authorise force after finding a threat to the peace, breach of the peace or act of aggression under Article 39. The earlier Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928 renounced war as an instrument of national policy, but it lacked the Charter's institutional machinery. In Nicaragua v. United States (ICJ, 1986) the Court treated the prohibition on the use of force as reflected in customary law as well as the Charter, and it held that only the gravest forms of force amount to an armed attack that triggers self-defence.

Jus in bello is a different system with a different logic. Its rules apply once an armed conflict exists, whether or not the conflict began lawfully. This is the principle of the equal application of IHL: the soldiers of an aggressor state and those of the state defending itself have the same rights and the same duties under the Geneva Conventions. The preamble of Additional Protocol I of 1977 states that the protections of the Conventions and of the Protocol must be applied without adverse distinction based on the nature or origin of the armed conflict or on the causes espoused by or attributed to the parties.

Why keep the two apart? If a belligerent's treatment of prisoners depended on whether its cause was just, every side would claim the just cause, and each would feel free to deny protection to the enemy. Humanitarian rules would collapse exactly when they are needed. Separation also reflects the reality that the protected people, wounded soldiers and civilians, did nothing to choose the war.

The separation has limits worth knowing. A state that violates jus ad bellum bears state responsibility and its leaders may face the crime of aggression, but that does not strip its soldiers of prisoner-of-war status. Likewise, a state acting in lawful self-defence still must obey distinction and proportionality; its right to respond does not authorise any means at all. Necessity and proportionality also appear in jus ad bellum, but there they ask whether the whole defensive response is justified, not whether a single strike on a particular building is lawful. Students often confuse the two uses of "proportionality," so keep the question straight: ad bellum proportionality concerns the scale of the response to the armed attack, in bello proportionality concerns expected civilian harm against the military advantage of a specific attack.

Worked example: State A invades State B in plain violation of Article 2(4). A captured A soldier is held by B. B may not mistreat or prosecute him merely for fighting in an unlawful war; he is entitled to prisoner-of-war treatment if he qualifies. A's leaders, however, may be accountable for aggression, and A owes reparation to B.

lessons.title: Sources: Hague Law, Geneva Law, Custom and the Martens Clause
body: IHL has two historical strands that are now largely merged. "Hague law" governs the means and methods of warfare: what weapons and tactics are permitted. Its landmark is the 1907 Hague Convention IV and its annexed Regulations respecting the laws and customs of war on land, which refined earlier work from 1899. "Geneva law" protects victims of war: the wounded, the sick, shipwrecked, prisoners and civilians. Its origins lie in Henri Dunant's experience after the battle of Solferino and the first Geneva Convention of 1864, and it reached its modern form in the four Geneva Conventions of 1949. Additional Protocol I of 1977 deliberately fused both strands by regulating the conduct of hostilities and protecting victims in one instrument.

The four 1949 Conventions cover: wounded and sick armed forces in the field (I), wounded, sick and shipwrecked armed forces at sea (II), prisoners of war (III) and civilians in the hands of an adversary (IV). They are among the most widely ratified treaties in the world, with participation essentially universal. The 1977 Additional Protocols are less widely accepted: Protocol I on international armed conflicts and Protocol II on non-international armed conflicts have many parties but not all states, and the United States, for example, signed both in 1977 without ratifying them. A third Protocol of 2005 added the red crystal as a protective emblem.

Customary law fills the gap. A rule of custom arises from consistent state practice accompanied by opinio juris, the belief that the practice is legally required. Custom binds states that are not party to a given treaty. In 2005 the ICRC published a study of customary IHL identifying a long list of rules, many of them applicable in both international and non-international conflicts. The study has been influential but not uncontroversial: some governments, including the United States in a formal response, challenged its methodology and some of its conclusions. A careful student treats it as a leading but contested reference.

The Martens clause is a safety net for situations the treaties do not cover. Drafted by the Russian jurist Friedrich Martens and placed in the preamble of the Hague conventions, it says that in cases not covered by specific rules, civilians and combatants remain under the protection of the principles of international law derived from established custom, the principles of humanity and the dictates of public conscience. It is repeated in Additional Protocol I, Article 1(2). Its legal effect is debated. The weak reading says it only confirms that custom continues to apply where treaties are silent. The strong reading says humanity and public conscience are independent sources of limits. Courts and states have used it cautiously, and the ICJ cited it in its 1996 advisory opinion on nuclear weapons.

Trap: do not say a treaty does not bind a non-party and stop there. The right question is whether the rule has also crystallised as custom, and whether the state persistently objected while the custom formed.

Worked example: Suppose State X has never ratified Additional Protocol I. It still may not deliberately attack civilians, because that prohibition is accepted as customary law, binding X whether or not X has joined the Protocol. If X also argued that the rule did not bind it, it would have to show that it persistently objected while the custom formed, which is very hard for a rule this widely accepted.

lessons.title: Classifying Conflicts: International, Non-International and the Thresholds
body: IHL does not apply to every act of violence. It applies when there is an armed conflict, and the type of conflict decides which treaty provisions govern. The Geneva Conventions use two categories.

International armed conflict (IAC) is addressed by common Article 2, which applies to declared war or any other armed conflict between two or more High Contracting Parties, even if a state of war is not recognised, and to cases of partial or total occupation, even without armed resistance. The threshold is low: resort to armed force between states is generally enough, and no minimum duration or intensity is required. Additional Protocol I, Article 1(4), also extends IAC rules to armed conflicts in which peoples fight against colonial domination, alien occupation and racist regimes in the exercise of self-determination, though this provision binds only parties to the Protocol and has little practical use today.

Non-international armed conflict (NIAC) is addressed by common Article 3, which applies to armed conflict not of an international character occurring in the territory of one party. The Conventions do not define it. The ICTY Appeals Chamber in Prosecutor v. Tadic (1995) supplied the standard formula: a NIAC exists whenever there is protracted armed violence between governmental authorities and organised armed groups, or between such groups within a state. Two elements are therefore used in practice: a minimum level of intensity and a minimum level of organisation of the non-state party. Internal disturbances such as riots, isolated and sporadic acts of violence and similar acts fall below the threshold, as Additional Protocol II, Article 1(2), explicitly states. Protocol II itself has a higher threshold than common Article 3: it requires that the armed group be under responsible command and exercise control over part of the territory so as to carry out sustained and concerted military operations and implement the Protocol.

Why does classification matter? The detailed regimes for prisoners of war and for occupation apply only in IACs. In NIACs, the treaty rules are thinner, though customary law has extended many conduct-of-hostilities rules to both categories. Classification can also be mixed. A conflict may be internationalised when another state intervenes, and courts have debated how much control over a rebel group a foreign state needs before the conflict becomes international. The ICJ in Nicaragua required effective control of specific operations to attribute rebel acts to a state, while the ICTY in Tadic preferred a looser overall control test for the purpose of classifying the conflict. The ICJ later reaffirmed effective control for the purposes of state responsibility.

Trap: a state that denies there is a "war" does not escape IHL. The legal test is factual. Governments often describe fighting as law enforcement or counter-terrorism, but if the facts meet the thresholds, IHL applies.

Worked example: Armed police clash with protesters for two days and several people die. The violence is serious but disorganised and sporadic, so no NIAC exists and human rights law and domestic criminal law govern. Months later, a well-organised group controls a district, fights government forces daily and holds prisoners. The Tadic standard is now met and common Article 3 applies.

lessons.title: Distinction, Proportionality and Precaution
body: Three principles structure the conduct of hostilities. They are codified in Additional Protocol I and are accepted as customary law.

Distinction (Articles 48, 51, 52). Parties must at all times distinguish between civilians and combatants and between civilian objects and military objectives, and direct attacks only at combatants and military objectives. Civilians are protected unless and for such time as they take a direct part in hostilities (Article 51(3)). Under Article 52(2), a military objective is an object which by its nature, location, purpose or use makes an effective contribution to military action and whose total or partial destruction, capture or neutralisation, in the circumstances ruling at the time, offers a definite military advantage. In case of doubt whether an object normally dedicated to civilian purposes, such as a school or house, is used for military action, it is presumed to be civilian (Article 52(3)). Indiscriminate attacks, those not directed at a specific military objective, using means that cannot be directed, or whose effects cannot be limited, are prohibited by Article 51(4). Using civilians as human shields is prohibited, and the presence of a shield does not remove the attacker's obligations (Article 51(7)).

Proportionality (Articles 51(5)(b) and 57(2)(a)(iii)). An attack is prohibited if it may be expected to cause incidental loss of civilian life, injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects that would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. Three features need care. First, the test applies to incidental harm; deliberately targeting civilians is not a proportionality question but a violation of distinction. Second, the standard is "excessive," not "any," so lawful attacks may kill civilians. Third, the judgment is made on information reasonably available to the commander at the time, not with hindsight. The two quantities are incommensurable, which critics note, and states have said that only clearly excessive imbalance is a violation, a threshold also found in the Rome Statute's war crime in Article 8(2)(b)(iv).

Precautions in attack (Article 57) and against the effects of attack (Article 58). Attackers must do everything feasible to verify that targets are military objectives, choose means and methods that minimise civilian harm, cancel or suspend an attack if it becomes apparent that it would violate the rules, and give effective advance warning of attacks that may affect the civilian population unless circumstances do not permit. Defenders must, to the extent feasible, remove civilians from the vicinity of military objectives and avoid locating military objectives within densely populated areas. Feasible means practicable given all circumstances at the time, including humanitarian and military considerations.

Worked example: A commander learns that an enemy ammunition store sits next to an apartment block. The store is a military objective. If an attack with a large bomb would be expected to kill many residents for the destruction of one depot, the commander must consider a smaller weapon, a different time of day, or a warning. If no feasible measure reduces the expected harm and the harm is still excessive relative to the advantage, the attack must not go ahead. If the same commander simply aims at the apartment block because enemy sympathisers live there, that is not a proportionality failure but a direct attack on civilians, a war crime.

lessons.title: The Wounded, the Sick, Medical Personnel and the Emblems
body: The oldest strand of humanitarian law protects those who can no longer fight. Geneva Convention I (1949) covers wounded and sick members of armed forces on land, and Convention II extends the same ideas to the wounded, sick and shipwrecked at sea. Their core rule is that such persons must be respected, collected and cared for without adverse distinction founded on sex, race, nationality, religion or political opinion. The only permissible ground for priority in treatment is urgent medical need (Convention I, Article 12). Parties must take all possible measures to search for and collect the wounded and to protect them against pillage and ill-treatment (Article 15).

Additional Protocol I generalises the idea in the notion of a person hors de combat (Article 41). A person is hors de combat if he is in the power of an adverse party, clearly expresses an intention to surrender, or has been rendered unconscious or is otherwise incapacitated by wounds or sickness and is therefore incapable of defending himself, provided that in each case he abstains from hostile acts and does not try to escape. Such a person may not be made the object of attack. Linked rules prohibit ordering that there shall be no survivors, or conducting hostilities on that basis, which is the prohibition of denial of quarter (Article 40), and protect parachutists leaving an aircraft in distress during their descent (Article 42).

Medical personnel, units and transports are protected because the healing mission benefits everyone. The protection depends on their exclusive assignment to medical purposes. They display the distinctive emblem: the red cross, the red crescent, and since Protocol III of 2005, the red crystal, all of which have the same legal value and are protective devices, not religious symbols. The emblem is the visible signal of a status the law already confers; a unit does not need to display it to be protected, but the display helps attackers identify it at a distance.

Protection can end, but only narrowly. Under Article 21 of Convention I, protection of fixed medical establishments and mobile units ceases if they are used outside their humanitarian duties to commit acts harmful to the enemy, and only after a warning that sets a reasonable time limit and goes unheeded. Several things do not count as acts harmful to the enemy: staff carrying light individual weapons for their own defence or that of the wounded in their charge, the presence of weapons collected from the wounded and not yet handed to the proper service, and the care of wounded combatants in the facility (Article 22). Using the emblem to cover military activity is perfidy, a serious violation, and it also harms the wider system of protection.

Trap: do not say that medical personnel become targets whenever they carry any weapon. Light personal arms used only for defence do not forfeit protection. Equally, do not say that a hospital cannot ever lose its protection; using a hospital as a firing position or arms store, after a warning, can.

Worked example: A field hospital flying the red cross is used by some soldiers as a mortar position. The attacking force cannot lawfully shell it at once. It must warn the occupants, fix a reasonable period for the misuse to stop, and attack only if the warning is ignored; even then it must apply proportionality and precautions for the wounded still inside, who remain protected persons.

lessons.title: Prisoners of War: Status, Treatment and Release
body: Prisoner-of-war (POW) status is a legal category, not a description of anyone who is captured. It exists only in international armed conflicts. Convention III, Article 4, lists the persons who qualify: members of the armed forces of a party and of militias or volunteer corps forming part of them, members of other militias and organised resistance movements belonging to a party who meet four conditions (a responsible commander, a fixed distinctive sign recognisable at a distance, arms carried openly, and conduct in accordance with the laws and customs of war), and inhabitants of unoccupied territory who spontaneously take up arms to resist an invasion, the levee en masse, if they carry arms openly and respect the laws of war. Additional Protocol I, Article 44, relaxes the rules for fighters in special situations where they cannot distinguish themselves, provided they carry arms openly during each engagement and while visible to the enemy in a deployment preceding an attack.

Status brings two things: combatant immunity, meaning a lawful combatant cannot be prosecuted merely for taking part in hostilities and for acts that comply with IHL, and the protections of captivity. If there is doubt about status, Article 5 says the person keeps POW treatment until a competent tribunal decides. Spies and mercenaries are not entitled to POW status (Protocol I, Articles 46 and 47), and a combatant who is captured while failing to distinguish himself from civilians in the way the law requires may lose it.

Treatment in captivity is governed by humane treatment as the master principle. Article 13 requires that POWs be humanely treated and protected against acts of violence, intimidation, insults and public curiosity, and it prohibits reprisals against them. They must be evacuated from the combat zone, housed in conditions no less favourable than the detaining power's own troops, and given adequate food, clothing and medical care. Interrogation is limited: a POW is bound to give only name, rank, date of birth and service number, and no physical or mental torture or any other form of coercion may be used to obtain more information (Article 17). Officers and other ranks can be required to work only under defined conditions, and prisoners may be punished only through the same courts and procedures that apply to the detaining power's own forces. The International Committee of the Red Cross must be allowed to visit them.

Captivity ends with release and repatriation without delay after the cessation of active hostilities (Article 118). The duty is not suspended by disputes over a peace treaty, and the Convention also requires direct repatriation of the seriously wounded and sick during the conflict. Transfer to another state is allowed only if that state is a party to the Convention and willing and able to apply it, and the transferring power stays responsible (Article 12).

What about those who fall outside the category? The Conventions have no term "unlawful combatant", and the label has been controversial. A person who is not a POW is not left without law. Civilians who are detained fall under Convention IV, and in all cases the fundamental guarantees of Protocol I, Article 75, and common Article 3 apply as a minimum. In Hamdan v. Rumsfeld (US Supreme Court, 2006), the Court held that common Article 3 applied to the armed conflict with al Qaeda, which it described as a conflict not of an international character, so that military commissions had to meet its requirement of a regularly constituted court.

Worked example: A uniformed soldier is captured by the enemy. He may be asked his name and rank and nothing more, must be moved from the front, may not be displayed to the press, may not be prosecuted for lawfully shooting enemy soldiers, and must be sent home once active hostilities end.

lessons.title: Civilians, Protected Persons and the Law of Occupation
body: Convention IV protects civilians who find themselves, in a conflict or occupation, in the hands of a party of which they are not nationals (Article 4). It has two main parts: general protections for the population against the consequences of war, and a detailed regime for aliens in the territory of a party and for people in occupied territory. Its basic standards include humane treatment, a ban on physical or moral coercion to obtain information, a prohibition on collective punishment, pillage and reprisals against protected persons, and a prohibition on taking hostages (Articles 27 to 34).

Occupation is a factual situation. Under Article 42 of the 1907 Hague Regulations, territory is occupied when it is actually placed under the authority of a hostile army, and the occupation extends only to the territory where that authority has been established and can be exercised. This is effective control without the consent of the local sovereign. In Armed Activities on the Territory of the Congo (DRC v. Uganda, ICJ, 2005), the Court found that Uganda was an occupying power in the Ituri district because its forces had substituted their own authority for the Congolese government's there, and that it was responsible for violations including looting and plunder of natural resources, both by its forces and for failing to prevent them in the territory it controlled.

The occupant is a temporary administrator, not a sovereign. It acquires no title to the territory, and Article 43 of the Hague Regulations requires it to take all measures in its power to restore and ensure public order and civil life, while respecting, unless absolutely prevented, the laws in force in the country. Convention IV adds that the penal laws of the occupied territory remain in force subject to limited exceptions for security and compliance (Article 64). Private property may not be confiscated, and pillage is prohibited (Hague Regulations, Articles 46 and 47). Public immovable property is held under a usufruct: the occupant may use it and its fruits but must safeguard the capital (Article 55). Destruction of property is prohibited except where rendered absolutely necessary by military operations (Convention IV, Article 53).

Two prohibitions generate the most controversy. Article 49 forbids individual or mass forcible transfers and deportations of protected persons from occupied territory, regardless of motive, although total or partial evacuation is allowed where the security of the population or imperative military reasons demand it. Article 49(6) provides that the occupying power shall not deport or transfer parts of its own civilian population into the territory it occupies. The ICJ in its 2004 Advisory Opinion on the Legal Consequences of the Construction of a Wall in the Occupied Palestinian Territory held Convention IV applicable there and treated settlements as contrary to Article 49(6); Israel disputes the applicability of the Convention to the territories and the interpretation of that provision. Rome Statute Article 8(2)(b)(viii) makes such transfers a war crime in international armed conflict.

Security detention is permitted only under strict conditions: internment or assigned residence is allowed only if absolutely necessary or, in occupied territory, for imperative reasons of security (Articles 42 and 78), with a right of appeal and periodic review by a competent body.
Trap: occupation law is not a licence to govern as the occupier wishes. It also continues for as long as effective control lasts, and it does not depend on a formal declaration of occupation.

Worked example: An occupying power closes a local radio station that broadcasts calls to arms against its troops. This may be justified for security under the penal and security powers. If it instead rewrites the territory's civil code to suit its own economic interests and settles its own citizens in the area, those acts conflict with the obligation to respect existing laws and with Article 49(6).

lessons.title: Non-International Armed Conflicts: Common Article 3, Protocol II and Custom
body: Most armed conflicts today are non-international, and the treaty law for them is much shorter than for wars between states. States were reluctant to regulate how they fight their own insurgents. The result is a small core, common Article 3, and a longer but less widely accepted Additional Protocol II.

Common Article 3 requires each party, including non-state armed groups, to treat humanely persons taking no active part in hostilities, including members of armed forces who have laid down their arms or are hors de combat through sickness, wounds or detention, without adverse distinction. It prohibits at any time and in any place violence to life and person (murder, mutilation, cruel treatment and torture), the taking of hostages, outrages upon personal dignity (in particular humiliating and degrading treatment), and passing sentences or carrying out executions without a judgment by a regularly constituted court affording the judicial guarantees recognised as indispensable. It also requires that the wounded and sick be collected and cared for, allows the ICRC to offer its services, and encourages special agreements bringing other provisions into force. The last sentence says that application does not affect the legal status of the parties, a clause meant to reassure governments that engaging with rebels does not grant them recognition.

Additional Protocol II develops these rules for conflicts that meet its higher threshold. It contains fundamental guarantees (Article 4, including a specific protection for children), rules on persons deprived of liberty (Article 5), penal prosecutions (Article 6), care of the wounded and sick and medical personnel (Articles 7 to 12), and protection of the civilian population (Articles 13 to 18), including a prohibition on attacking civilians, on starvation as a method of combat (Article 14) and on forced displacement unless civilian security or imperative military reasons require it (Article 17).

Custom has done much of the bridging. In Tadic (1995), the ICTY Appeals Chamber held that many rules of the law of international conflicts had come to apply in internal ones, including the protection of civilians and rules on means and methods of warfare, and that serious violations of common Article 3 can entail individual criminal responsibility. The ICRC customary law study reaches similar conclusions for many rules. The Rome Statute lists war crimes in non-international conflicts separately, in Article 8(2)(c) for violations of common Article 3 and 8(2)(e) for other serious violations.

Several gaps remain. First, there is no prisoner-of-war status and no combatant immunity in a non-international conflict. Fighters of an armed group can be prosecuted under domestic law for taking up arms, though they cannot be punished for war crimes without a fair trial and, as noted in Protocol II, Article 6(5), authorities are encouraged at the end of hostilities to grant the broadest possible amnesty to those who took part in the conflict or are deprived of liberty for reasons related to it. The ICRC reads this as excluding persons suspected of war crimes. Second, the treaty text says little about the legal basis and procedures for detention by either side. Third, the question of how armed groups are bound is debated; the common explanations are that they are bound because the state of which they are nationals is bound, because they exercise government-like functions, or because customary law binds all parties.

Trap: describing a captured rebel as a "prisoner of war" is a classification error. In a non-international conflict he is a detainee entitled to humane treatment and fair trial, but not to POW status.

Worked example: A rebel group executes captured soldiers after a "trial" by its commander without any independent court. This violates common Article 3's ban on sentences without a regularly constituted court and, as murder of persons hors de combat, is a war crime under Rome Statute Article 8(2)(c)(i).

lessons.title: Weapons Law: General Principles and Specific Treaties
body: Weapons law rests on two general rules. The first is that the right of parties to choose methods or means of warfare is not unlimited (Additional Protocol I, Article 35(1), echoing the Hague Regulations). The second has two limbs: a ban on weapons and methods that are of a nature to cause superfluous injury or unnecessary suffering (Article 35(2), whose lineage goes back to the 1868 St Petersburg Declaration), and a ban on weapons that are indiscriminate by nature because they cannot be directed at a specific military objective or their effects cannot be limited (Article 51(4)). Superfluous injury asks whether the harm to combatants exceeds what any legitimate military purpose requires; indiscriminate weapons concern civilians. Note that a weapon is not unlawful merely because it is terrible. The issue is whether harm is unnecessary relative to its military purpose.

On top of these principles sits a patchwork of specific treaties. The Geneva Gas Protocol of 1925 bans the use in war of asphyxiating, poisonous or other gases and bacteriological methods. The Biological Weapons Convention of 1972 prohibits developing, producing and stockpiling biological and toxin weapons, but it has no standing verification body. The Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993, in force since 1997, goes further: it bans the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons and creates an organisation (the OPCW) to verify destruction and inspect. The 1980 Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons and its Protocols restrict, among others, non-detectable fragments, mines and booby-traps, incendiary weapons, and (Protocol IV of 1995) laser weapons specifically designed to cause permanent blindness. The 1997 Ottawa Convention bans anti-personnel mines, and the 2008 Convention on Cluster Munitions bans cluster munitions of the kind it defines, though a number of major military powers have not joined either treaty. Treaties bind only parties, so non-parties remain subject to the general rules and any customary prohibitions, such as the widely accepted prohibition on the use of chemical weapons.

Nuclear weapons are governed by a particular blend of law. In its 1996 Advisory Opinion on the Legality of the Threat or Use of Nuclear Weapons, the ICJ found no comprehensive and universal prohibition in customary or treaty law, held that any threat or use must comply with IHL and would generally be contrary to its rules, and said it could not conclude definitively whether use would be lawful or unlawful in an extreme circumstance of self-defence in which the very survival of a state was at stake. It also unanimously affirmed an obligation to pursue negotiations on nuclear disarmament in good faith. The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, adopted in 2017 and in force since 2021, bans them for its parties, but the states possessing nuclear weapons are not among them.

States must also look at weapons before they use them. Article 36 of Additional Protocol I requires a state party, when studying, developing, acquiring or adopting a new weapon, means or method of warfare, to determine whether its employment would be prohibited. Many states without the Protocol conduct such reviews as a matter of practice.

Trap: do not equate "banned" with "dangerous". Many lawful weapons are very destructive. A weapon is prohibited by a specific treaty, because it is by nature indiscriminate, or because it causes unnecessary suffering. Even a lawful weapon may be used unlawfully, for instance when it is aimed at civilians.

Worked example: A state develops a munition that scatters tiny bomblets over a wide area, many of which fail to explode. Review proceeds on two tracks: whether a specific treaty, such as the Cluster Munitions Convention, forbids it for that state, and whether general principles forbid it as indiscriminate in the areas where it would be used, taking into account the risk to civilians from unexploded remnants.

lessons.title: Methods of Warfare: Perfidy, Starvation, Cultural Property and the Environment
body: Methods of warfare are the tactics used. Several are restricted or prohibited by rules of general application.

Perfidy versus ruses. Additional Protocol I, Article 37, prohibits killing, injuring or capturing an adversary by resort to perfidy: acts inviting the confidence of an adversary to lead him to believe that he is entitled to, or obliged to accord, protection under the rules of armed conflict, with intent to betray that confidence. Examples are feigning an intent to negotiate under a flag of truce or to surrender, feigning incapacitation by wounds or sickness, feigning civilian status, and feigning protected status by using signs of the United Nations or of neutral states. Ruses of war, by contrast, are lawful: camouflage, decoys, mock operations and false information are meant to mislead but do not invoke legal protection. The test is whether the deception exploits a duty the law imposes on the adversary to refrain from attack. A fighter who hides in foliage uses a ruse; a fighter who raises a white flag and then opens fire commits perfidy. Perfidy that causes death or injury is a war crime, and the misuse of the distinctive emblems is separately prohibited (Article 38).

Starvation and relief. Article 54 prohibits starvation of civilians as a method of warfare and attacking, destroying, removing or rendering useless objects indispensable to the survival of the civilian population, such as foodstuffs, crops, livestock and drinking water installations, for the specific purpose of denying them to civilians. Rome Statute Article 8(2)(b)(xxv) makes intentional use of starvation as a method of warfare a war crime in international armed conflicts, including wilfully impeding relief supplies. In December 2019 the Assembly of States Parties adopted an amendment adding a parallel offence for non-international conflicts (Article 8(2)(e)(xix)). Under Article 121(5) it binds only states parties that have accepted it; it entered into force on 14 October 2021 and, as of October 2026, about 25 states have accepted it, so the Court's reach over starvation in a non-international conflict depends on whether the state concerned is one of them. Sieges are not unlawful as such, but a besieging party may not use starvation of civilians as a method of war, and relief operations that are humanitarian and impartial must be allowed, subject to agreement of the parties concerned, which may not be arbitrarily withheld (Article 70). In 2018 the Security Council, in Resolution 2417, condemned starving civilians as a method of warfare.

Cultural property. The 1954 Hague Convention and its two Protocols (1954 and 1999) oblige parties to safeguard cultural property in peacetime and respect it in war, which means refraining from use of it for military purposes and from directing hostilities against it, subject to a waiver for imperative military necessity whose conditions are tightened in the Second Protocol. Additional Protocol I, Article 53, separately protects historic monuments, works of art and places of worship that constitute the cultural or spiritual heritage of peoples. In Prosecutor v. Al Mahdi (ICC, 2016), the accused pleaded guilty to the war crime of intentionally directing attacks against religious and historic buildings, namely mausoleums and a mosque in Timbuktu, Mali, and was sentenced to nine years.

The natural environment. Articles 35(3) and 55 of Protocol I prohibit methods or means of warfare intended or expected to cause widespread, long-term and severe damage to the natural environment. The words are cumulative and the threshold is deliberately high, so that few conflicts have met it. The Rome Statute covers environmental damage only where it is clearly excessive in relation to the concrete and direct overall military advantage (Article 8(2)(b)(iv)). A separate 1976 treaty, ENMOD, prohibits hostile use of environmental modification techniques having widespread, long-lasting or severe effects. Outside these provisions, the environment is protected indirectly as a civilian object.

Worked example: Soldiers approach an enemy position holding up their hands as if to surrender, and when the defenders stand to take them prisoner they throw grenades. This is perfidy: it exploits the defenders' duty to accept surrender. A different unit that places inflatable tank decoys in a field to attract enemy bombers has used a lawful ruse.

lessons.title: Targeting in Practice: Direct Participation, Dual-Use Objects, Cyber Operations and Autonomy
body: Real conflicts are messy: fighters do not wear uniforms, civilian infrastructure serves armies, and weapons increasingly rely on software. IHL answers by applying the same principles with careful tests, though several of those tests are contested.

Direct participation in hostilities. Civilians are protected from attack unless and for such time as they take a direct part in hostilities (Article 51(3)). The ICRC's 2009 Interpretive Guidance proposed three cumulative conditions: the act must be likely to adversely affect military operations or inflict harm on protected persons or objects (threshold of harm); there must be a direct causal link between the act and the harm in a single causal step (direct causation); and the act must be designed to support one party and harm another (belligerent nexus). Examples include shooting at soldiers or laying roadside bombs; merely paying taxes, selling food to soldiers or expressing support does not qualify. For members of an organised armed group, the Guidance suggests that a "continuous combat function" makes a person targetable for as long as he holds it, even when not actively fighting. Many states and scholars criticise parts of the Guidance, particularly the time and membership issues, so treat it as influential but disputed. A civilian who has taken part regains protection once the participation ends, and in cases of doubt the person is to be considered civilian (Article 50(1)).

Dual-use objects. Some objects serve both military and civilian purposes: a power plant, a bridge, a telecommunications network. There is no separate category of "dual-use object" in the treaties. Each is assessed under Article 52(2): if its use makes an effective contribution to military action and its destruction offers a definite military advantage, it is a military objective, and the civilian side then enters the proportionality and precaution analysis. Being a military objective does not mean any attack is lawful. Destroying a grid that also supplies hospitals can cause severe indirect civilian harm that must be counted among the foreseeable effects.

Cyber operations. There is broad agreement among states that IHL applies to cyber operations that occur in the context of an armed conflict. The hard question is what counts as an attack and as an object. An operation expected to cause death, injury or physical damage is clearly an attack. Operations that disable a network without physical damage, or that delete civilian data, are debated: some states and the ICRC argue that loss of functionality should count, while others require physical effects. The Tallinn Manual, written by independent experts at the invitation of a NATO centre, is a respected academic restatement but is not a treaty and does not bind states.

Autonomous weapon systems. These are systems that select and engage targets without further human intervention. No treaty specifically regulates them as of October 2026. A Group of Governmental Experts under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons has developed a draft "rolling text" of elements of an instrument and is due to report to the CCW's Seventh Review Conference in November 2026, which will decide on next steps; the UN General Assembly has also considered the subject. There is wide agreement that existing IHL applies, including weapons review under Article 36, and that distinction, proportionality and precautions require human judgment that cannot simply be delegated. Contested questions include how much human control is required, who bears responsibility for an unlawful strike, and whether a specific prohibition or regulation is needed.

Worked example: A hacker group not formally part of the armed forces ceases to be protected only while it carries out acts that meet the three conditions, for example by disabling an air defence system for a military operation. Selling antivirus software to the same army would not count, though it may support the war effort.

lessons.title: Compliance and Enforcement: Grave Breaches, Universal Jurisdiction and Responsibility
body: IHL has no police force, so compliance depends on a layered system. At the base is the obligation in common Article 1 of the Geneva Conventions for states to respect and to ensure respect for the Conventions in all circumstances. The second limb is generally read to oblige states to use lawful means to encourage others to comply and not to assist violations, though the precise reach of that duty is debated. Armed forces must be trained in IHL and have legal advisers, and commanders must ensure subordinates know the rules.

The Conventions create a special regime for grave breaches. Each Convention lists acts, if committed against protected persons or property, that are grave breaches. Under Convention IV (Article 147) these include wilful killing, torture or inhuman treatment, wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury, unlawful deportation or transfer, unlawful confinement, compelling a protected person to serve in hostile forces, taking hostages, and extensive destruction and appropriation of property not justified by military necessity. Additional Protocol I, Article 85, adds, among others, launching an indiscriminate attack affecting civilians with knowledge that it will cause excessive loss, and the transfer by an occupier of its own population. Parties must enact legislation, search for persons alleged to have committed or ordered such breaches, and bring them before their own courts regardless of nationality, or hand them over for trial to another party with a prima facie case (Convention IV, Article 146). This obligation to prosecute or extradite is the basis of universal jurisdiction in treaty terms. Strictly, the grave breaches regime applies to international armed conflicts, though customary law and later tribunals have extended war crimes liability to non-international conflicts. For other violations, states must take measures necessary to suppress them.

Universal jurisdiction lets a state prosecute certain crimes regardless of where they occurred or the nationality of the perpetrator or victim. National courts have used it in recent years, but it is politically sensitive and often restricted by domestic law or prosecutorial discretion. Immunity is a major limit. In Arrest Warrant of 11 April 2000 (DRC v. Belgium, 2002), the ICJ held that an incumbent foreign minister enjoys immunity from the criminal jurisdiction of other states, including for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, while in office, but stressed that immunity from jurisdiction is not impunity. A person may be prosecuted by his own state, if his state waives immunity, once he leaves office for acts committed in a private capacity or before or after the term, or before an international court whose statute provides for it. How far the rule applies to former officials and to acts in an official capacity is debated.

State responsibility sits beside individual responsibility. A state that violates IHL commits an internationally wrongful act for which it owes cessation and reparation; Hague Convention IV (Article 3) and Additional Protocol I (Article 91) say a party is liable to pay compensation for violations by persons forming part of its armed forces. Reprisals, once the classic enforcement tool, are now heavily restricted: they are prohibited against protected persons under the Conventions and against civilians and civilian objects, cultural property, objects indispensable to survival, the environment and works containing dangerous forces under Protocol I. Other mechanisms include the ICRC's role in visiting detainees, the Protecting Power system (rarely used), and the Protocol I fact-finding commission, which has seen little use.

Worked example: A visiting foreign minister is accused of ordering torture of civilians at home. A third state may not arrest him for trial while he holds office, but a tribunal with jurisdiction might, or his own state could prosecute, or immunity could be waived. After he leaves office, a court may be able to act depending on the conduct and the court's rules.

lessons.title: The Nuremberg and Tokyo Legacy
body: Before 1945, international law was mostly addressed to states. Individuals who committed atrocities were punished, if at all, by their own governments or by the victors under national military law. The Nuremberg trials changed the premise: individuals can bear criminal responsibility directly under international law, and official position is no shield.

The International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg was created by the London Agreement and Charter of 8 August 1945 among the United States, the United Kingdom, France and the Soviet Union. Its Charter gave jurisdiction over three categories: crimes against peace (planning, preparing, initiating or waging a war of aggression or a war in violation of international treaties, including participation in a common plan or conspiracy to do so), war crimes (violations of the laws and customs of war), and crimes against humanity (murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation and other inhumane acts against civilians, and persecutions on political, racial or religious grounds, in execution of or in connection with the other crimes in the tribunal's jurisdiction). Twenty-four leaders were indicted and twenty-two were tried in the main proceedings; judgments were delivered at the end of September and on 1 October 1946, with twelve death sentences and three acquittals. Several organisations were also declared criminal. A parallel tribunal for the Far East, the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, sat in Tokyo from 1946 and delivered judgments in 1948, with one judge, Radhabinod Pal of India, dissenting on important points. Twelve further trials of doctors, judges, industrialists and others were held by US tribunals at Nuremberg under Control Council Law No. 10.

The legal contributions were large. The Tribunal rejected the defence of superior orders as a complete defence (it could at most mitigate punishment), rejected the argument that acts of state shielded officials, and treated the crimes as committed by individuals, not abstract entities. The UN General Assembly affirmed the principles of the Charter and judgment in 1946, and the International Law Commission formulated seven Nuremberg Principles in 1950.

The trials were also criticised then and since. The first objection is "victors' justice": the judges came only from the victorious powers, and Allied conduct, including the Soviet role in the invasion of Poland, was not tried. The second is nullum crimen sine lege, the principle that no one should be punished for conduct that was not criminal when committed, which was raised against crimes against peace and crimes against humanity. The Tribunal answered that the principle is one of justice and not a limit on sovereignty, that the Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928 had already made aggressive war illegal, and that those who attacked their neighbours in knowing violation of treaties could not claim surprise. Critics remain unconvinced on crimes against humanity, which had a weaker pre-1945 pedigree. In practice, the Tribunal tied crimes against humanity to the other crimes in its jurisdiction, a link later dropped.

A related precedent is In re Yamashita (US Supreme Court, 1946), in which a Japanese general was convicted by a US military commission for failing to control troops who committed atrocities in the Philippines. It is a landmark of command responsibility but is also criticised for the thinness of the findings on his knowledge and control.

The post-war period also produced the Genocide Convention of 1948, the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and the Nuremberg legacy of personal accountability, which fed into the later ad hoc tribunals and the ICC.

Worked example: A minister argues that he cannot be tried because he acted as head of a department under orders from the head of state. Under the Nuremberg principles, neither official position nor superior orders is a complete defence; the orders may be considered only in mitigation where justice requires.

lessons.title: Individual and Command Responsibility: Modes of Liability and Defences
body: International crimes are usually committed by groups and organisations. The law therefore needs doctrines that reach people at every level. The Rome Statute is the most systematic statement. Article 25(3) lists forms of individual responsibility: committing a crime, whether individually, jointly with another or through another person; ordering, soliciting or inducing it; aiding, abetting or otherwise assisting, including by providing the means; and contributing to the commission of a crime by a group acting with a common purpose, with the aim of furthering the group's criminal activity or with knowledge of its intent. Direct and public incitement is separately covered for genocide, and attempts are punishable. Article 27 says official capacity is irrelevant: heads of state and ministers are not exempt from responsibility or entitled to a reduction in sentence on that ground. Article 29 provides that crimes within the Court's jurisdiction are not subject to any statute of limitations.

Joint criminal enterprise (JCE) was developed by the ICTY Appeals Chamber in Prosecutor v. Tadic (1999) as a form of liability for participants in a common plan, drawing on post-war cases. It distinguishes forms by the participants' mental state, including an extended form for foreseeable crimes outside the plan. It was criticised as too broad, and the ICC has used different concepts, such as co-perpetration based on control over the crime.

Superior or command responsibility is different in kind. Under Article 28 of the Rome Statute, a military commander (or person effectively acting as one) is criminally responsible for crimes committed by forces under his effective command and control, or effective authority and control, as a result of his failure to exercise control properly, if he either knew or, owing to the circumstances at the time, should have known that the forces were committing or about to commit such crimes, and failed to take all necessary and reasonable measures within his power to prevent or repress their commission or to submit the matter to the competent authorities. The standard for civilian superiors is stricter on knowledge: the superior must have known or consciously disregarded information which clearly indicated that the subordinates were committing or about to commit the crimes, and the crimes must concern activities within his effective responsibility and control. The key concept is effective control, meaning the material ability to prevent or punish, which the ICTY applied in Celebici (Trial Chamber 1998, affirmed 2001). Responsibility under Article 28 is for failure to supervise, which is often argued as a form of liability for the crimes of others, not a separate offence.

In Prosecutor v. Bemba Gombo, an ICC Trial Chamber convicted a Congolese politician in 2016 under Article 28 for crimes committed by his militia in the Central African Republic. In 2018 the Appeals Chamber, by majority, reversed the conviction, holding among other things that the Trial Chamber had erred in assessing whether Bemba took all necessary and reasonable measures given his limited ability to act from abroad. It remains an important illustration that the "reasonable measures" element is judged on what was actually possible for the commander.

Superior orders and other defences. Article 33 states that a person who commits a crime pursuant to an order of a government or superior is not relieved of responsibility unless he was under a legal obligation to obey, did not know the order was unlawful, and the order was not manifestly unlawful; orders to commit genocide or crimes against humanity are manifestly unlawful. Article 31 recognises grounds for excluding responsibility, including mental disease, intoxication in limited cases, self-defence or defence of others (with a proportionality requirement and, for war crimes, defence of property essential for survival or a mission), and duress. Mistakes of fact or law may negate the mental element. Article 26 excludes persons under eighteen at the time of the alleged crime from the Court's jurisdiction.

Worked example: A general knows his troops are looting villages and executing prisoners, receives reports each week, and takes no steps to stop them or to refer the cases for prosecution. He may be responsible under command responsibility for the crimes. A private soldier who obeyed an order to shoot unarmed civilians cannot rely on superior orders, because the order was manifestly unlawful.

lessons.title: War Crimes: Grave Breaches, Serious Violations and the Rome Statute List
body: A war crime is a serious violation of the laws and customs applicable in armed conflict that entails individual criminal responsibility. Not every violation of IHL is a war crime; the violation must be serious (endangering protected persons or objects, or breaching important values) and, under customary law, individual responsibility must attach.

Article 8 of the Rome Statute organises war crimes into four groups. For international armed conflicts: (a) grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, such as wilful killing, torture or inhuman treatment, wilfully causing great suffering, extensive destruction of property not justified by military necessity, unlawful deportation or confinement, and taking hostages; and (b) other serious violations of the laws and customs applicable in international armed conflict, a long list including intentionally directing attacks against the civilian population or against civilians not taking direct part in hostilities, intentionally directing attacks against civilian objects, launching an attack knowing it will cause incidental civilian harm clearly excessive in relation to the concrete and direct overall military advantage anticipated (Article 8(2)(b)(iv)), attacking undefended towns, pillaging, using poison or prohibited gases, killing or wounding treacherously, improper use of emblems, transfer by an occupying power of parts of its own civilian population into occupied territory, and conscripting or enlisting children under fifteen or using them to participate actively in hostilities. For non-international armed conflicts: (c) serious violations of common Article 3, and (e) other serious violations of laws and customs, a shorter list that includes attacks on civilians, on medical and

humanitarian personnel, on protected buildings, pillage, sexual violence, and the use of child soldiers. Article 8(2)(d) and (f) fix the threshold: non-international conflict provisions do not cover internal disturbances, and they apply to protracted armed conflict between governmental authorities and organised armed groups or between such groups.

Article 8(1) says the Court shall have jurisdiction over war crimes "in particular" when committed as part of a plan or policy or as part of a large-scale commission. The words are a guide to the Court's focus and not a strict element, though the Court has used them in selecting cases. A war crime must have a nexus to an armed conflict: the conduct must take place in the context of and be associated with it, and the perpetrator must be aware of the factual circumstances establishing that the conflict exists. The victims must also be protected persons or objects under the relevant rule.

The first judgment of the ICC was Prosecutor v. Lubanga Dyilo (2012), in which a Trial Chamber convicted the Congolese militia leader of the war crimes of conscripting and enlisting children under the age of fifteen and using them to participate actively in hostilities in an armed conflict not of an international character. The conviction was upheld on appeal in 2014. The case illustrates the nexus requirement, the NIAC list, and the Court's treatment of child soldiers, including that "participation" extends beyond direct combat to roles exposing children to danger as targets.

War crimes can be prosecuted nationally and internationally, and the grave breaches regime requires states to prosecute or extradite. Some experts argue that the distinction between grave breaches and other war crimes is a historical artefact that has lost most of its meaning.

Trap: do not confuse a violation of the proportionality rule with a war crime. The Rome Statute requires that the harm be clearly excessive, and that the perpetrator know the attack will cause such harm, a much higher bar than the treaty rule in Additional Protocol I.

Worked example: A battalion commander orders artillery on a village he knows contains only civilians, to punish residents for supporting the enemy. This is intentionally directing attacks against civilians, a war crime in both international and non-international conflicts, and no proportionality calculation arises.

lessons.title: Crimes Against Humanity and Genocide
body: Crimes against humanity and genocide are both crimes that may be committed in peacetime or in armed conflict. They differ in what they protect and in the intent they require.

Crimes against humanity. Article 7 of the Rome Statute defines them as listed acts committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against any civilian population, with knowledge of the attack. The acts include murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation or forcible transfer of population, imprisonment in violation of fundamental rules of international law, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence of comparable gravity, persecution against an identifiable group on political, racial, national, ethnic, cultural, religious, gender or other grounds in connection with another act or crime in the Statute, enforced disappearance, apartheid, and other inhumane acts of a similar character causing great suffering or serious injury. "Widespread" refers to large scale or number of victims; "systematic" to an organised pattern. The attack is a course of conduct involving multiple commission of the acts against a civilian population, pursuant to or in furtherance of a State or organisational policy to commit the attack (Article 7(2)(a)). The single act of the accused need not be widespread, but it must form part of the attack, and he must know of it. Unlike at Nuremberg, no link to armed conflict is required under the Rome Statute, and no discriminatory intent is required except for persecution. There is currently no stand-alone treaty on crimes against humanity;

the International Law Commission adopted draft articles in 2019. In December 2024 the General Assembly (resolution 79/122) decided to convene a conference of plenipotentiaries, with negotiating sessions planned for 2028 and 2029, so a convention has not yet been concluded as of October 2026.

Genocide. The 1948 Convention (Article II) defines genocide as any of five acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such: killing members of the group; causing serious bodily or mental harm; deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about physical destruction in whole or in part; imposing measures intended to prevent births; and forcibly transferring children of the group to another group. The Rome Statute repeats the definition in Article 6. Two features define the crime. First, the special intent (dolus specialis) to destroy the group as such, in addition to the intent to commit the underlying act. Second, the protected groups are limited to the four listed; political and social groups are not covered, a gap noted by many critics. "In whole or in part" has been interpreted to require a substantial part. Genocide is also punishable when committed through conspiracy, direct and public incitement, attempt, or complicity (Article III), and states have duties to prevent and punish (Article I).

The ICJ in Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro (2007) held that genocide was committed at Srebrenica in July 1995, that Serbia had not committed genocide through its organs or direction and control of the perpetrators, nor conspired or was complicit, but that Serbia had breached its obligation to prevent genocide and failed to cooperate with the ICTY. The case shows that state responsibility for genocide is a separate question from individual criminal responsibility, and that the duty to prevent depends on a state's capacity to influence the perpetrators. Later ICJ cases on genocide, such as Croatia v. Serbia (2015), found no genocide on the facts.

How to tell them apart on an exam: a massacre of civilians as part of a government campaign may be a crime against humanity even if its victims are a political group; to be genocide it must target a protected group with intent to destroy it. A single crime can also be both. Persecution is often confused with genocide: persecution requires a discriminatory purpose but not the intent to destroy.

Worked example: A regime rounds up members of an ethnic minority, kills the men and sends the children to be raised in other communities, with statements declaring the aim of eliminating the group from the region. The facts support genocide, through the acts of killing and the forcible transfer of children, and also crimes against humanity.

lessons.title: The Ad Hoc and Hybrid Tribunals: ICTY, ICTR and Beyond
body: After Nuremberg and Tokyo, international criminal justice lay dormant for almost half a century. The wars in the former Yugoslavia and the genocide in Rwanda revived it. The UN Security Council, acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, created the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) by Resolution 827 in 1993 and the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) by Resolution 955 in 1994. These are called ad hoc tribunals because each was created for a particular situation, with limited temporal and territorial jurisdiction. Their statutes covered genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war (and, for Rwanda, violations of common Article 3 and Additional Protocol II). Primacy was a notable feature: they could request national courts to defer to them, the reverse of the ICC's complementarity. Both completed their work and closed in the 2010s, and a residual body, the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals, continues functions such as appeals and enforcement.

In Prosecutor v. Tadic, the ICTY Appeals Chamber's 1995 decision on jurisdiction was foundational. It held that the Security Council had power under Chapter VII to establish the tribunal as a measure to maintain or restore peace, that the conflict could be treated as both international and internal for the purposes of the statute, and that serious violations of common Article 3 and other rules for internal conflicts can be prosecuted as war crimes under customary law. This ruling was a major step towards the modern law of war crimes in non-international conflicts.

The ICTR's Prosecutor v. Akayesu (1998) was the first conviction for genocide by an international tribunal after a trial. The Trial Chamber found a mayor guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity, and held that rape and sexual violence can constitute acts of genocide when committed with intent to destroy a protected group, as well as crimes against humanity. At the ICTY, key proceedings included the trials of Slobodan Milosevic, who died in custody in 2006 before judgment, Radovan Karadzic (convicted in 2016, with the sentence increased to life imprisonment on appeal in 2019 before the Residual Mechanism) and Ratko Mladic (life imprisonment in 2017, upheld on appeal in 2021). The ICTY Appeals Chamber in Krstic (2004) held that the killing of the men of Srebrenica amounted to genocide, a finding the ICJ later shared.

Hybrid or internationalised tribunals combine international and domestic elements, in staffing, law or both. The Special Court for Sierra Leone, created by agreement between the UN and the government, convicted Liberia's former president Charles Taylor in 2012 of aiding and abetting war crimes and crimes against humanity; the Appeals Chamber affirmed in 2013. The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia tried leaders of the Khmer Rouge, and in 2018 convicted Nuon Chea of genocide against the Vietnamese and Cham groups and Khieu Samphan of genocide against the Vietnamese group only, among other crimes. Nuon Chea died in 2019 before his appeal was decided, and in 2022 the Supreme Court Chamber affirmed Khieu Samphan's convictions and life sentence. Other examples include the Special Tribunal for Lebanon and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The tribunals had strengths and limits. They built a large body of case law on command responsibility, joint criminal enterprise, sexual violence and the elements of crimes, and they showed that heads of state could be tried. Critics point to cost and duration, the distance from affected communities, and perceived selectivity, as when the ICTY chose not to open an investigation into NATO's 1999 bombing campaign. Defenders say the tribunals contributed to documenting events and shaping the Rome Statute.
Trap: do not confuse the Security Council-created ICTY and ICTR, which had primacy over national courts, with the ICC, created by treaty and based on complementarity.

Worked example: A state refuses to hand over a suspect sought by the ICTY. Because the tribunal was created under Chapter VII, states were obliged to cooperate with it under the Council's binding resolution, a source of authority that the ICC, a treaty body, lacks for non-parties.

lessons.title: The International Criminal Court: Structure and Jurisdiction
body: The Rome Statute was adopted on 17 July 1998 and entered into force on 1 July 2002. It created a permanent court, seated in The Hague, to try individuals for the most serious crimes of concern to the international community. It is a treaty body: it binds only its states parties, which numbered 125 according to the UN Secretary-General as depositary in early October 2026, although important states including the United States, Russia, China, India and Israel are not parties. Several states have signed but later declared they would not become parties. Withdrawal takes effect one year after notice (Article 127), and several notices are pending: Niger, Burkina Faso and Mali (June 2026), Venezuela and Chad (July 2026) and Nauru (September 2026), each effective one year later. If all take effect, the number of parties will fall to 119. Burundi and the Philippines have already withdrawn, and Hungary withdrew its 2025 notice of withdrawal in May 2026, so it remains a party.

Structure. The Court has four organs: the Presidency, the Chambers (Pre-Trial, Trial and Appeals divisions, with eighteen judges), the Office of the Prosecutor, and the Registry. The Assembly of States Parties oversees management and the budget. Victims may participate in proceedings and seek reparations, and the Trust Fund for Victims supports them. The maximum sentence is thirty years, or life imprisonment where justified by the extreme gravity of the crime (Article 77).

Subject-matter jurisdiction (Article 5) covers genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. Temporal jurisdiction is prospective only: the Court cannot try crimes committed before the Statute entered into force for the state concerned (Article 11). The Court has no jurisdiction over persons under eighteen at the time of the crime (Article 26).

Preconditions (Article 12). Where a situation reaches the Court through a state party referral or by the Prosecutor's own initiative, the Court may act only if the crime was committed on the territory of a state party (including on its vessels or aircraft), or by a national of a state party. A non-party may also accept jurisdiction for a specific situation by lodging a declaration (Article 12(3)). This is why a national of a non-party can be investigated if he commits crimes on the territory of a state party.

Trigger mechanisms (Article 13). There are three: a referral of a situation by a state party; a referral by the Security Council acting under Chapter VII, which can reach non-parties without the Article 12 preconditions (as with Darfur in Resolution 1593 of 2005 and Libya in Resolution 1970 of 2011); and an investigation opened by the Prosecutor on her own initiative (proprio motu), which requires authorisation by a Pre-Trial Chamber (Article 15). The Security Council may also, by a Chapter VII resolution, request the Court to defer an investigation or prosecution for twelve months, renewable (Article 16).

The crime of aggression. The Statute listed aggression in Article 5 but left its definition and conditions for later. At the 2010 Review Conference in Kampala, states adopted amendments defining the crime of aggression (Article 8 bis) and setting conditions for jurisdiction (Article 15 bis and ter). The Court's jurisdiction was activated on 17 July 2018. For state-party referrals and proprio motu investigations, the regime is narrower than for other crimes: it does not cover aggression by nationals or on the territory of non-parties, and states parties may opt out by declaration. Security Council referrals are not subject to these limits. The crime requires a leader, defined as a person in a position effectively to exercise control over or direct the political or military action of a state, and an act of aggression that, by its character, gravity and scale, constitutes a manifest violation of the UN Charter.

Worked example: A national of a non-party state commits a war crime on the territory of a state party. The Court may exercise jurisdiction because the crime occurred on a party's territory, even though the accused's state never joined. If the same person committed the crime in a non-party state, the Court could act only if that state lodged an Article 12(3) declaration or the Security Council referred the situation.

lessons.title: Complementarity, Admissibility, Cooperation and Immunities
body: Complementarity is the principle that the ICC complements, and does not replace, national criminal jurisdictions. The preamble says it, and Article 1 establishes the Court "complementary to national criminal jurisdictions." States keep the primary responsibility to investigate and prosecute, and the Court steps in only when they fail.

Article 17 sets the admissibility test. A case is inadmissible where it is being investigated or prosecuted by a state which has jurisdiction over it, unless the state is unwilling or unable genuinely to carry out the investigation or prosecution; where a state with jurisdiction has investigated and decided not to prosecute, unless the decision resulted from unwillingness or inability; or where the person has already been tried for the conduct (see also Article 20 on ne bis in idem), and where the case is not of sufficient gravity. Unwillingness is assessed by looking at whether proceedings are or were undertaken for the purpose of shielding a person from responsibility, whether there has been an unjustified delay inconsistent with an intent to bring the person to justice, or whether proceedings are not independent or impartial. Inability concerns a total or substantial collapse or unavailability of the national judicial system. The key word is "genuinely": a sham domestic process does not block the Court, and a real one, even if it reaches a different result, does.

Procedure follows from this. When the Prosecutor opens an investigation, she notifies states parties and states that would normally exercise jurisdiction, and a state may inform the Court within a month that it is investigating, in which case the Prosecutor defers unless the Pre-Trial Chamber authorises the investigation (Article 18). A state, an accused or a state whose consent is required may challenge admissibility or jurisdiction (Article 19). In practice, the principle also encourages "positive complementarity", in which the Court's existence prompts national reform and prosecutions.

Cooperation. The ICC has no police. It relies on states parties to arrest and surrender suspects and to provide evidence (Part 9 of the Statute). Non-party states are not obliged unless the Security Council has required it. Non-cooperation is a persistent weakness: several warrants have remained unexecuted for years.

Immunities. Article 27 removes the relevance of official capacity before the Court. But Article 98(1) states that the Court may not proceed with a request for surrender or assistance that would require a state to act inconsistently with its obligations under international law regarding the state or diplomatic immunity of a person or property of a third state, unless the Court first obtains the third state's cooperation for a waiver. The reconciliation of these provisions has been contested. In the Al-Bashir proceedings, concerning the sitting President of Sudan, the Court issued warrants in 2009 (war crimes and crimes against humanity) and 2010 (genocide, added). When Jordan failed to arrest him in 2017 on a visit, the Appeals Chamber held in 2019 that there is no rule of customary international law recognising head-of-state immunity vis-a-vis an international court, and that Jordan had failed to comply with its obligations. The reasoning was influential but has been criticised by some commentators, who note differences between that holding and the ICJ's reasoning in the Arrest Warrant case about national courts.

The Prosecutor and the Court must also manage a limited budget and a vast number of potential cases. Selection of situations and cases involves prosecutorial discretion, guided by the gravity of the crimes, the interests of victims and, under Article 53, the "interests of justice."

Worked example: State S is investigating a general for a massacre, but its prosecutors are removed whenever they approach the general and the file has been dormant for ten years. The ICC may find that S is unwilling genuinely to prosecute, because of unjustified delay and lack of independence, and rule the case admissible. If S instead is conducting real trials, even leading to an acquittal, the case remains inadmissible.

lessons.title: Accountability Debates: Selectivity, Amnesties, Universal Jurisdiction and Peace
body: International criminal justice is contested. This lesson separates the law as it stands from the debates about it, and presents the main positions at their strongest. As of this writing, several of the situations mentioned are ongoing and developing, so check current sources.

What the law provides. The Court can act only within its jurisdiction: crimes on the territory of states parties or by their nationals, situations referred by the Security Council, or by consent of a non-party. States have primary responsibility to prosecute. There is no international rule by treaty that blanket amnesties for the gravest crimes are always void, but the Statute of the Special Court for Sierra Leone expressly stated that amnesties granted would not bar prosecution, and in its 2004 decision in Kallon and Kamara the Court held that the Lome Accord amnesty did not bar prosecution for international crimes. Many UN bodies and human rights courts take the view that amnesties for genocide, crimes against humanity and serious war crimes are impermissible. The Rome Statute is silent on amnesties; Article 53 allows the Prosecutor to decline to proceed where it would not serve the interests of justice. Immunities and universal jurisdiction are as discussed above, and national courts have used universal jurisdiction in some cases. For example, in 2022 a German court at Koblenz convicted a former Syrian intelligence officer of crimes against humanity and sentenced him to life imprisonment.

Debate 1: selectivity. Critics argue that the Court's caseload has been dominated by African situations while powerful states and their allies have escaped scrutiny, and that the Security Council's power of referral and deferral, with the veto, politicises the process. Defenders reply that many African situations were referred by the states themselves, that the Prosecutor has since opened investigations elsewhere, and that imperfect enforcement is not a reason to prosecute no one. Recent warrants have generated sharp disputes. On 17 March 2023 the Court issued warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova for the alleged war crimes of unlawful deportation and transfer of children from occupied areas of Ukraine to Russia. On 21 November 2024 it issued warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes (including starvation as a method of warfare) and crimes against humanity in the situation in Palestine, and for Mohammed Deif of Hamas; proceedings against Deif were terminated on 26 February 2025 after the Prosecution notified the Chamber of his death. On 8 July 2025 it issued warrants for the Taliban's Supreme Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and Chief Justice Abdul Hakim Haqqani for the alleged crime against humanity of persecution on gender grounds. These are allegations at the warrant stage, not findings of guilt. Some states reject the Court's
jurisdiction or the legitimacy of the proceedings, others emphasise equal application of the law, and the matters are still developing.

Debate 2: peace versus justice. One position holds that threats of prosecution can prolong conflicts by removing the incentive for leaders to negotiate their exit, and that amnesties, truth commissions and national processes may secure more peace. The opposing position holds that impunity breeds further atrocity, that victims have a right to justice, and that sustainable peace requires accountability. Compromise models, such as Colombia's transitional justice system with reduced sanctions in exchange for full confession, test whether conditional accountability satisfies complementarity.

Debate 3: sovereignty and non-parties. The United States has long opposed the Court's jurisdiction over nationals of non-parties and has concluded bilateral agreements and imposed sanctions on Court officials in some periods. Supporters of the Court point to the territorial basis of jurisdiction, which is a standard principle of criminal law.

Debate 4: effectiveness. Detractors point to a small number of convictions relative to the Court's cost and the problems of arrest. Supporters stress deterrent and normative effects, the role of national prosecutions it prompts, and the role of the Court in victim participation and reparations.

Trap: do not mistake a debate for a rule. That the Court's legitimacy is contested does not alter the legal question of whether it has jurisdiction over a given situation, and that a state rejects jurisdiction does not by itself decide the matter.

Worked example: After a civil war, a government offers an amnesty covering all combatants, including those accused of mass killings of civilians. Under the SCSL's approach, and the view of most UN bodies, the amnesty would not prevent prosecution for crimes under international law before an international court, though it could be relevant to the ICC's "interests of justice" assessment or to the question of genuine national proceedings.
